items.title: Counting seconds
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
When I brew my coffee, I generally do it in 4 parts. One is the blooming phase, I pour 50ml and wait until it's all gone through.

Then I do three other 50ml pours with 10 seconds between each.

To count these 10 seconds, I use crocodiles, like so: "Un crocodile, deux crocodiles, trois crocodiles,...".

Crocodile is the word we use in the french speaking part of Belgium. I think I have seen Americans use Mississippi as well.

I'll use this note as a way to compile all different manners of counting in seconds from around the world. If you could send me an email to tell me how it's done in your part of the world, I'd be very pleased.

Crocodile: Wallonia

Mississippi: USA

items.title: A gut feeling is only as reliable as the memory behind it
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

That feeling that you’re onto something, the one that turns up before you can explain it, doesn’t come from nowhere. Your memory is running ahead of your conscious mind. It picks up a pattern, calls up what it already knows about it, and tells you that things hang together well before you could say what they are.

Take something as simple as a drawing torn into scraps. You can’t tell what it shows, but you sense that the lines make up something meaningful, and you guess right more often than chance would predict. The shape of the scraps isn’t what guides you. It’s the concept they’ve stirred up in your memory, which never quite rises to the surface. Turn the same drawing upside down, with exactly the same scraps, and the hunch vanishes, because it no longer matches anything you have stored.

The practical upshot is that an intuition is worth no more than the experience behind it. In a field you know well, a first hunch is information in compressed form, and it’s…

🫧 Open on Bubbles

On May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread . I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that.

However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/. The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post.

Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way.

items.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
items.label: Hobbies and Creative
items.excerpt:
Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

items.title: Circular Reference In A Set Causes Stack Overflow In Adobe ColdFusion 2025
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
I'm working on an algorithm that walks over the nodes of a complex data structure in ColdFusion. Anytime you traverse a data structure manually, you run the risk of infinite recursion if there's a cycle somewhere in the bowels of the given data tree. Now that Adobe ColdFusion 2025 update 8 introduced Sets as a new data type, I thought maybe I could use a Set to store a manifest of "nodes visited". This way, if I inspect a data node that's already in the Set, I'll know that I've hit a circular reference.

Unfortunately, it seems that putting a circular reference into a Set causes ColdFusion to throw a stack overflow error. Looking at the stack trace, it appears to go crazy in the .hashCode() calls. Which makes sense if ColdFusion is using .hashCode() to determine a unique identifier for each object.

items.title: Feed the Scorchpot [$14.99] [Strategy] [Windows] [macOS]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.

Cook cleverly, plan badly, or just roll with it — the dragon doesn't care how you win, only that you feed the beast on time. And yes, you can pet the…
